title: Online Learning and the Ed Tech Debate

reader_summary.headline: Hi and welcome to the A16Z podcast.
reader_summary.overview: Hi and welcome to the A16Z podcast. I'm Lauren Murrow, and today's episode is all about education and technology. Much of the discussion has been in the context of COVID and safety. In this episode, A16Z general partner Connie Chan and I are joined by educators and experts Josh Kim.

key_points.text: I'm Lauren Murrow, and today's episode is all about education and technology.
key_points.evidence_quote: I'm Lauren Murrow, and today's episode is all about education and technology, a topic that's especially top of mind as students in much of the country are returning to school this week, virtually.

key_points.text: Much of the discussion has been in the context of COVID and safety.
key_points.evidence_quote: Much of the discussion has been in the context of COVID and safety, but there's a greater debate around ed tech's potential that's been decades in the making.

key_points.text: In this episode, A16Z general partner Connie Chan and I are joined by educators and experts Josh Kim.
key_points.evidence_quote: In this episode, A16Z general partner Connie Chan and I are joined by educators and experts Josh Kim, the director of online programs and strategy at the Dartmouth Center for the Advancement of Learning.

key_points.text: His most recent book, Learning Innovation and the Future of Higher Education, was published earlier this year, and David Deming.
key_points.evidence_quote: His most recent book, Learning Innovation and the Future of Higher Education, was published earlier this year, and David Deming, Professor of Education and Economics at the Harvard Kennedy School and the Harvard Graduate School of Education.

thesis: The episode argues that the spring emergency pivot to remote learning due to COVID should not be used as the basis for judging the quality or potential of online education. Instead, the discussion emphasizes that online education is a mode of delivery with tremendous potential to reach people and offer better curriculum than in-person models, particularly for specific age groups and content types like singing classes, rather than being an abject failure.
